title: Lower limb neurological examination: L4, L5 and S1 roots

guidelineVersions: GIRFT national suspected cauda equina pathway (updated Mar 2026)

related.id: MB-155 History: back pain with red flags
related.why: The cauda equina questions and emergency pathway

brief.scenario: Mrs Sarah Dalby, 47, a care assistant, has had low back pain radiating down her left leg for six weeks since lifting a resident. The top of her left foot feels numb, and she has started catching her toes on the stairs.
brief.task: Perform a neurological examination of her lower limbs. You will be stopped at 6 minutes to present your findings and answer questions.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Gait, look, tone, power, reflexes, sensation, root tension; then the cauda equina screen.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Naming a root without testing the muscles that separate L5 from a peroneal nerve palsy.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Could you walk to the door and back for me, then on your heels and on your toes?"

flow: Straight leg raise; cauda equina screen

grid.label: Preparation and exposure
grid.pass: Introduces, confirms identity, gains consent, asks about pain, and exposes both legs while keeping her covered.
grid.high: Explains each step before doing it and compares both sides throughout.

grid.label: Gait and inspection
grid.fail: Starts power testing without watching her walk or looking at the legs.
grid.pass: Watches her walk, including on heels and toes; inspects for wasting, fasciculation, scars and foot posture.
grid.high: Uses heel walking to show weak dorsiflexion and toe walking to screen plantarflexion before she lies down.

grid.label: Tone and power, graded
grid.fail: Tests 'push and pull' at the ankle only, without grading.
grid.pass: Tests tone, then hip flexion, knee extension, ankle dorsiflexion, great toe extension and plantarflexion on both sides, graded 0–5.
grid.high: Adds ankle inversion and hip abduction to separate an L5 root lesion from a common peroneal nerve palsy.

grid.label: Reflexes and plantars
grid.fail: Omits reflexes or the plantar response.
grid.pass: Tests knee and ankle reflexes, with reinforcement if absent, and plantar responses, comparing sides.
grid.high: Links reflexes to roots: a reduced knee jerk points to L4, a reduced ankle jerk to S1; normal reflexes fit L5.

grid.label: Sensation by dermatome
grid.fail: Tests sensation vaguely up and down the leg.
grid.pass: Tests light touch and pinprick at the key points: medial malleolus (L4), dorsum of foot at the third MTP joint (L5), lateral heel (S1).
grid.high: Maps the edge of the numb area and says whether it matches the L5 dermatome or a peripheral nerve territory.

grid.label: Root tension and cauda equina screen (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Doesn't ask about saddle numbness, bladder or bowel symptoms.
grid.pass: Performs straight leg raise on both sides; asks about saddle numbness, bladder, bowel and sexual function; records perianal sensation.
grid.high: States that a rectal examination isn't necessary, but perianal sensation must be recorded.

grid.label: Presentation at the signal
grid.fail: Lists the tests without naming a level.
grid.pass: Presents the positive and negative findings and names the root: left L5 radiculopathy.
grid.high: Leads with the level, then the key negatives: normal reflexes, no upper motor neurone signs, no cauda equina features.

grid.label: Next steps and red flags (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Treats new saddle numbness or bladder change as routine.
grid.borderline: Knows cauda equina syndrome is an emergency but plans a routine outpatient MRI.
grid.pass: No red flags: keeps her active, avoids gabapentinoids and oral steroids; requests MRI, because her motor deficit makes it likely to change management.
grid.high: Suspected cauda equina: emergency MRI as soon as possible and within 4 hours of the request; nil by mouth; senior discussion.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: [Starts testing power with her trousers on.] Push against my hand.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: [Pushes and pulls at both ankles.] That's a bit weak.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: [No reflexes.] Can you feel this? [Strokes up and down the leg.]

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: She has weakness and some numbness in the left leg.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: She mentions she's numb when she wipes since yesterday. What now?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd book an MRI in the next few weeks.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hello, I'm Dr Kaur, one of the surgical trainees. Can I check your name and date of birth? I'd like to examine the nerves in your legs. Any pain now? Could you change into shorts? [Consent; cleans hands.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Walk to the door and back, then on your heels, then on your toes. [Inspects both legs for wasting, fasciculation and scars.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [Rolls legs; knee lift.] Now push against me. [Hip flexion, knee extension, ankle dorsiflexion, great toe extension, plantarflexion; grades each.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [Light touch and pinprick at the medial malleolus, top of the foot and lateral heel, both sides.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [Straight leg raise, both sides.] Any numbness around your bottom, or change in your bladder or bowels? [Records perianal sensation.] Thank you. [Cleans hands.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Mrs Dalby has weak left ankle dorsiflexion and great toe extension, reduced sensation over the dorsum of the left foot, normal reflexes, and a positive left straight leg raise. This is a left L5 radiculopathy. No cauda equina symptoms.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: With no red flags, I'd keep her active and avoid gabapentinoids and oral steroids. She has a motor deficit, so an MRI is likely to change management; I'd request one.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hello, I'm Dr Kaur, one of the surgical trainees. Can I check your name and date of birth? I'll explain each step and compare both legs. Could you change into shorts? [Cleans hands.]

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Heel walking.] The left heel drops: weak dorsiflexion. [Toe walking normal.] So plantarflexion is probably strong.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Grades each movement.] Left ankle dorsiflexion 4, great toe extension 4. Inversion and hip abduction are also 4, so this isn't just the common peroneal nerve: it's the L5 root.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Reflexes with reinforcement.] Knee and ankle jerks normal and equal, plantars flexor. That fits L5, not L4 or S1.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Maps the numb area.] It covers the dorsum of the foot, including the key point at the third MTP joint; the medial malleolus and lateral heel are normal: L5 dermatome.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Straight leg raise.] Left positive. I'd ask about saddle numbness, bladder, bowel and sexual function, and record perianal sensation; a rectal examination isn't necessary. [Cleans hands.]

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Mrs Dalby has a left L5 radiculopathy: weak dorsiflexion, great toe extension, inversion and hip abduction, with numbness in the L5 dermatome. Reflexes are normal, there are no upper motor neurone signs and no cauda equina features.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: She mentions she's numb when she wipes since yesterday. What now?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That's suspected cauda equina syndrome. She needs an emergency MRI as soon as possible and within 4 hours of the request, stays nil by mouth, and I'd discuss her with my senior now.

failures.consequence: An L5 root lesion can't be told apart from a common peroneal nerve palsy.

failures.move: Testing sensation without reference to dermatomes.
failures.consequence: The level can't be named, so the presentation has no conclusion.

failures.move: Leaving out the cauda equina questions.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: early saddle or bladder symptoms are missed, and the chance to decompress before permanent loss passes.

failures.move: Booking a routine MRI for new saddle numbness.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: the pathway requires an emergency MRI within 4 hours of the request.

recovery.when: You forgot the cauda equina questions
recovery.line: Before I finish, have you noticed any numbness around your bottom, or any change in your bladder or bowels?

recovery.when: The examiner asks about a rectal examination
recovery.line: It isn't necessary for suspected cauda equina, but I'd record perianal sensation.

knowledge.fact: Key muscles: L4 ankle dorsiflexion, L5 great toe extension, S1 plantarflexion. Key sensory points: L4 medial malleolus, L5 dorsum of foot at the third MTP joint, S1 lateral heel.
Tibialis posterior (inversion) is L4–L5 via the tibial nerve, so weak inversion points to the root, not the common peroneal nerve.
Suspected cauda equina: emergency MRI as soon as possible and within 4 hours of request; no rectal examination needed; record perianal sensation.

Sciatica: no gabapentinoids, other antiepileptics, oral steroids or benzodiazepines. In specialist care, image only if the result is likely to change management. Consider decompression if non-surgical care fails and imaging matches.

recall.think: Which root, and is this cauda equina syndrome?
recall.say: "Weak great toe extension and inversion, numb dorsum, normal reflexes: left L5 radiculopathy."
do: Grade power; add inversion and hip abduction

numbers.meaning: emergency MRI for suspected CES, from request

recall.trap: Normal reflexes don't mean normal roots: L5 has no routinely tested reflex.
recall.finish: No red flags: NICE NG59 care; red flags: emergency MRI and spinal referral.

sources.name: ICBSE Guide to the intercollegiate MRCS examination
sources.supports: Introduce yourself, confirm identity, obtain consent and clean hands at every station; 6-minute signal in examination stations

sources.name: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery (O'Connell, McCaskie, Sayers, eds)
sources.supports: Neurological examination sequence; heel and toe walking; reflex root values (knee L3–L4, ankle S1); straight leg raise

sources.name: Rupp R, et al. International Standards for Neurological Classification of Spinal Cord Injury: Revised 2019. Top Spinal Cord Inj Rehabil 2021;27(2):1–22 (ASIA/ISCoS worksheet REV 04/19)
sources.supports: Key muscles: L2 hip flexors, L3 knee extensors, L4 ankle dorsiflexors, L5 long toe extensors, S1 ankle plantar flexors; key sensory points: L4 medial malleolus, L5 dorsum of the foot at the third metatarsophalangeal joint, S1 lateral heel

sources.name: Medical Research Council: Aids to the examination of the peripheral nervous system (Memorandum No. 45)
sources.version: 1976 reprint (Memorandum No. 45) of the 1943 original; UKRI online version published 15 January 2016
sources.supports: 0–5 scale for recording muscle power (0 no contraction, 1 flicker, 2 movement with gravity eliminated, 3 against gravity, 4 against gravity and resistance, 5 normal); root values: quadriceps L2–L4, tibialis anterior L4–L5 (deep peroneal nerve), extensor hallucis longus L5–S1 (deep peroneal), tibialis posterior L4–L5 (tibial nerve), gluteus medius L4–S1 (superior gluteal nerve), gastrocnemius and soleus S1–S2

sources.name: GIRFT (NHS England): Spinal surgery: National suspected cauda equina syndrome (CES) pathway
sources.supports: Back or leg pain plus recent onset (14 days or fewer) or deterioration of urinary difficulty, altered perianal, perineal or genital sensation, severe or progressive neurological deficit of both legs, loss of rectal fullness or sexual dysfunction warrants emergency referral to the nearest hospital with emergency MRI; digital rectal examination not necessary but subjective perianal sensation should be recorded; bladder scans not to be used in isolation or as a discriminator in deciding to request an MRI; emergency MRI as soon as possible and certainly within four hours of request; keep nil by mouth; discuss with a senior (ST4 or above); new bilateral sciatica without CES symptoms: urgent (two-week) MSK triage and safety-netting

sources.name: NICE NG59: Low back pain and sciatica in over 16s: assessment and management
sources.supports: Think about alternative diagnoses and exclude specific causes (1.1.1); do not routinely image in a non-specialist setting (1.1.4); consider imaging in specialist settings only if the result is likely to change management (1.1.6); do not offer gabapentinoids, other antiepileptics, oral corticosteroids or benzodiazepines for sciatica (1.2.16); consider epidural local anaesthetic and steroid in acute and severe sciatica (1.3.5); consider spinal decompression when non-surgical treatment has not improved pain or function and imaging is consistent with the symptoms (1.3.8)

media.task: Optional: revise the key sensory points

partner.opening: Please examine this patient's lower limbs neurologically. I'll stop you at 6 minutes.
partner.actorBrief: You are Mrs Sarah Dalby, 47, a care assistant. Your back and left leg have hurt for six weeks since you lifted a resident. The pain runs down the outside of your left leg to the top of your foot, which feels numb. You catch your left toes on the stairs. No numbness around your bottom, no bladder, bowel or sexual problems, and your right leg is fine. When the left leg is raised straight, say it sends pain down the leg. When walking on your heels, let the left front of the foot drop.

reveals.trigger: Watches gait, heel and toe walking
reveals.finding: Mild slapping of the left foot. Can't hold the left forefoot up when heel walking. Toe walking normal.
No wasting, fasciculation or scars. Normal foot posture.
Tone normal. Right leg 5/5 throughout. Left: hip flexion 5, knee extension 5, ankle dorsiflexion 4, great toe extension 4, ankle inversion 4, eversion 4, hip abduction 4, plantarflexion 5.
Knee and ankle jerks present and equal. Plantars flexor. No clonus.
Reduced light touch and pinprick over the dorsum of the left foot, including the third MTP joint point. Medial malleolus and lateral heel normal. Right normal.
Left: pain below the knee at about 40 degrees. Right: no pain.

reveals.trigger: Asks about saddle, bladder, bowel and sexual symptoms
reveals.finding: None. Perianal sensation reported as normal.
Say: "Please stop there and present your findings."

push.question: Which root, and why?
push.expect: Left L5: weak great toe extension and dorsiflexion, numb dorsum of foot, normal reflexes.

push.question: How would you tell this from a common peroneal nerve palsy?
push.expect: Inversion (tibialis posterior, tibial nerve) and hip abduction are weak in an L5 root lesion but spared in a peroneal palsy.

push.question: How would you manage her?
push.expect: Keep active; no gabapentinoids, oral steroids or benzodiazepines; MRI, as the motor deficit makes it likely to change management; decompression considered if non-surgical care fails and imaging matches.

curveballs.prompt: Since yesterday she's numb when she wipes and has trouble starting to pass urine.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Suspected cauda equina syndrome: emergency MRI as soon as possible and within 4 hours of the request; nil by mouth; senior discussion.

curveballs.prompt: Should you do a rectal examination?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Not necessary; record perianal sensation. Don't use a bladder scan alone, or as a discriminator, to decide on MRI.

curveballs.prompt: Her ankle jerk is absent, plantarflexion is weak and the lateral heel is numb.
Her sciatica has become bilateral, but she has no cauda equina symptoms.
curveballs.safeAnswer: A warning sign: urgent (two-week) MSK triage referral, with a safety-net card and advice to return immediately with any cauda equina symptom.
